entries.content_plain:
CHAPTER 38
 
Ge 38:1-30. Judah and Family.

1. at that time--a formula frequently used by the sacred writers, not to describe any precise period, but an interval near about it.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv437"/><div sID="gen639" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv437"/><hi type="bold">2. And Judah saw there a daughter of a certain Canaanite--</hi>Like Esau [Ge 26:34], this son of Jacob, casting off the restraints of religion, married into a Canaanite family; and it is not surprising that the family which sprang from such an unsuitable connection should be infamous for bold and unblushing wickedness. <div eID="gen639" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 2. Judah said unto Onan ... marry her, and raise up seed to thy brother--</hi>The first instance of a custom, which was afterwards incorporated among the laws of Moses, that when a husband died leaving a widow, his brother next of age was to marry her, and the issue, if any, was to be served heir to the deceased (compare <reference osisRef="Deut.25.5">De 25:5</reference>). <div eID="gen640" type="x-p"/>

Judah ... went up unto his sheep-shearers--</hi>This season, which occurs in Palestine towards the end of March, was spent in more than usual hilarity, and the wealthiest masters invited their friends, as well as treated their servants, to sumptuous entertainments. Accordingly, it is said, Judah was accompanied by his friend Hirah.<div eID="gen641" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen642" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Timnath--</hi>in the mountains of Judah. <div eID="gen642" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain:
12. Judah ... went up unto his sheep-shearers--This season, which occurs in Palestine towards the end of March, was spent in more than usual hilarity, and the wealthiest masters invited their friends, as well as treated their servants, to sumptuous entertainments. Accordingly, it is said, Judah was accompanied by his friend Hirah.
 
Timnath--in the mountains of Judah.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv440"/><div sID="gen643" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv440"/><hi type="bold">18. signet, &c.--</hi>Bracelets, including armlets, were worn by men as well as women among the Hebrews. But the Hebrew word here rendered "bracelets," is everywhere else translated "lace" or "ribbon"; so that as the signet alone was probably more than an equivalent for the kid, it is not easy to conjecture why the other things were given in addition, except by supposing the perforated seal was attached by a ribbon to the staff. <div eID="gen643" type="x-p"/>

But the Hebrew word here rendered "bracelets," is everywhere else translated "lace" or "ribbon"; so that as the signet alone was probably more than an equivalent for the kid, it is not easy to conjecture why the other things were given in addition, except by supposing the perforated seal was attached by a ribbon to the staff.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv441"/><div sID="gen644" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv441"/><hi type="bold">24. Bring her forth, and let her be burnt--</hi>In patriarchal times fathers seem to have possessed the power of life and death over the members of their families. The crime of adultery was anciently punished in many places by burning (<reference osisRef="Lev.21.9">Le 21:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Judg.15.6">Jud 15:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.29.22">Jr 29:22</reference>). This chapter contains details, which probably would never have obtained a place in the inspired record, had it not been to exhibit the full links of the chain that connects the genealogy of the Saviour with Abraham; and in the disreputable character of the ancestry who figure in this passage, we have a remarkable proof that "He made himself of no reputation" [Php 2:7]. <chapter eID="Gen.38"/>
entries.content_plain: 24. Bring her forth, and let her be burnt--In patriarchal times fathers seem to have possessed the power of life and death over the members of their families. The crime of adultery was anciently punished in many places by burning (Le 21:9; Jud 15:6; Jr 29:22). This chapter contains details, which probably would never have obtained a place in the inspired record, had it not been to exhibit the full links of the chain that connects the genealogy of the Saviour with Abraham; and in the disreputable character of the ancestry who figure in this passage, we have a remarkable proof that "He made himself of no reputation" [Php 2:7].
